subtopic_detail: Recurrent disproportionate aggressive outbursts with normal interepisode function and genuine remorse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old electrician referred by his employer after he punched a hole through a plasterboard wall when a delivery arrived late. He has had about two shouting outbursts a week for the past year and three episodes of breaking his own property.

He describes the outbursts as coming on within seconds, being over within half an hour, and leaving him ashamed and apologetic. He gains nothing from them and has never planned one. Between episodes his mood is steady, he sleeps well, he holds down his job and he has close friendships he values.

data_table.History: No history of deliberate deception, theft, cruelty or disregard for others' rights before age 15, no self harm, no fear of abandonment, no unstable self image
data_table.Substance history: Drinks 4 standard drinks on a Friday night only, no illicit drug use, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no pressured speech, no grandiosity, no psychotic features, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Intermittent explosive disorder
options.rationale: Recurrent verbal or behavioural outbursts that are grossly out of proportion to the provocation, are impulsive rather than premeditated, occur at the required frequency, and are followed by remorse in someone who functions normally between episodes meet the diagnostic criteria. The outbursts must not be better explained by another disorder, which the history here systematically excludes. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder
options.rationale: This requires a pervasive pattern of disregard for the rights of others with evidence of conduct disorder before age 15, including deceitfulness, exploitation and lack of remorse. His aggression is confined to discrete impulsive episodes and he experiences shame afterwards, which is the opposite of the characteristic absence of remorse. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Bipolar disorder with mixed features
options.rationale: Irritability in bipolar disorder occurs within a sustained mood episode lasting days, accompanied by changes in sleep, energy, speech, goal directed activity and self esteem. His outbursts last under an hour with entirely normal mood, sleep and function in between, which is incompatible with a mood episode. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Borderline personality disorder
options.rationale: Anger dyscontrol is one of nine criteria, but the diagnosis requires a broader pattern including unstable relationships, identity disturbance, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, chronic emptiness and self harm. He has stable friendships, a stable self image and none of the other features. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Alcohol induced mood disorder
options.rationale: A substance induced disorder requires the symptoms to occur during intoxication or withdrawal, and his drinking is limited to one evening a week while the outbursts occur twice weekly and unrelated to alcohol. A negative drug screen and normal liver function further reduce the likelihood. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Intermittent explosive disorder is diagnosed when impulsive aggressive outbursts recur out of proportion to provocation, either as verbal or non-destructive outbursts twice weekly for three months, or as three episodes involving damage or injury within a year. The aggression must be impulsive and not committed to achieve a tangible objective, which separates it from instrumental aggression, and the person must be at least 6 years old developmentally. It is largely a diagnosis of careful exclusion: mood episodes, personality disorders, substance effects, acquired brain injury and, in younger patients, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder all need to be considered. It is more common than generally recognised, is associated with substantial occupational, legal and relationship harm, and responds to cognitive behavioural therapy focused on relaxation, cognitive restructuring and coping skills, with fluoxetine having the best evidence among medications.
key_points: Outbursts are impulsive, disproportionate and not committed for tangible gain
Normal function and mood between episodes is required
Remorse after episodes argues against antisocial personality disorder
Mood episodes last days, not minutes, which excludes bipolar disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with fluoxetine the best evidenced medication
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about conduct problems before age 15 and about what the person feels immediately after an outburst: premeditated aggression for gain with no remorse points to antisocial personality disorder, while impulsive aggression followed by shame points to intermittent explosive disorder.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Next line treatment for treatment resistant depression when lithium and quetiapine augmentation are unsuitable
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42 year old accountant with a moderate depressive episode that has persisted for 11 months. He has completed 8 weeks of escitalopram 20 mg daily and 10 weeks of venlafaxine 225 mg daily, both at full dose with good adherence, alongside 14 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy.

A quetiapine trial 6 months ago was stopped after he gained 9 kg in 7 weeks and was too sedated to work. He continues to work full time, has no psychotic features, is eating and sleeping adequately and denies any thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive but persistently low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no delusions or hallucinations, no suicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Rating scale: Montgomery Asberg Depression Rating Scale 26, indicating moderate severity
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 132 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits, no history of seizures or intracranial metal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Refer urgently for a course of electroconvulsive therapy
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective treatment available and is prioritised for depression with psychotic features, catatonia, food refusal, high suicide risk or life threatening severity, none of which are present. It also requires general anaesthesia and causes anterograde and retrograde memory effects that would be hard to reconcile with continuing full time professional work. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Augment with lithium and monitor levels and renal function
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation has good evidence in treatment resistant depression and would otherwise be a strong choice, but an eGFR of 44 mL/min/1.73m2 puts him in the group where lithium clearance is reduced, toxicity risk is increased and further renal decline is a genuine concern. Renal impairment is the finding that removes this option rather than any lack of efficacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add quetiapine 50 mg at night as an augmenting agent
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is an evidence based option, but he has already failed quetiapine on tolerability with clinically significant weight gain and sedation. Rechallenging with the same agent predictably reproduces the adverse effects that ended the previous trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
options.rationale: He meets the Australian funding criteria for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, having failed two adequate antidepressant trials at therapeutic dose and duration alongside psychological therapy, with no seizure history and no intracranial ferromagnetic material. It requires no anaesthetic, does not impair cognition and is delivered as outpatient sessions, so he can continue working through the course. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different class
options.rationale: Remission rates fall substantially with each successive antidepressant switch, and after two adequate failed trials a further switch has a materially lower expected yield than augmentation or a device based treatment. It is a defensible option but not the highest value next step once two full trials have failed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Treatment resistant depression is usually defined as failure to respond to two or more antidepressants given at adequate dose for adequate duration with confirmed adherence, and the first task is always to verify that both of those conditions were actually met and that the diagnosis is right. Once genuine resistance is established, the options are augmentation with lithium or a second generation antipsychotic, switching class, device based treatments including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroconvulsive therapy, and newer agents such as esketamine in specialist settings. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation has been funded in Australia since late 2021 for adults with treatment resistant major depression who have failed two adequate medication trials and received psychological therapy, and it occupies the space between medication augmentation and electroconvulsive therapy. Electroconvulsive therapy remains the most effective option and moves to the front of the queue when there is psychosis, catatonia, food refusal or imminent risk.
key_points: Confirm adequate dose, adequate duration and adherence before labelling resistance
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is funded after two failed adequate trials plus psychological therapy
It needs no anaesthetic and does not cause the cognitive effects of electroconvulsive therapy
Electroconvulsive therapy takes precedence with psychosis, catatonia, food refusal or high risk
Reduced renal function is a practical barrier to lithium augmentation
explanation.pearls: Screen for seizure history, intracranial metal, cochlear implants and cardiac devices before referring for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, since seizure induction is the main serious adverse event and occurs in fewer than 1 in 10,000 treatment sessions.

subtopic_detail: Functional seizures with atypical semiology and repeated normal routine electroencephalograms
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman who has had events described as seizures for 2 years, now occurring up to five times a week. She takes levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and reports no reduction in frequency on either.

Her partner has filmed an event. It lasts 9 minutes, with her eyes squeezed tightly shut throughout, side to side head movements, and thrashing of the arms and legs that is out of phase between the two sides. Afterwards she is immediately oriented and tells you she could hear her partner talking to her during it. She has never bitten her tongue and has never been incontinent.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no injuries or scarring, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with epilepsy protocol reported as normal, two routine interictal electroencephalograms normal, serum prolactin taken 20 minutes after an event within normal limits, electrolytes and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add sodium valproate as a third antiseizure medication
options.rationale: Adding a third agent assumes a diagnosis of epilepsy that the semiology and investigations increasingly contradict, and it exposes a woman of reproductive age to the most teratogenic antiseizure medication available. Escalating treatment is the commonest way these patients accumulate years of unnecessary drug exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for prolonged video electroencephalographic monitoring
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient video monitoring captures a typical event with simultaneous electroencephalographic recording and is the diagnostic standard for distinguishing functional seizures from epilepsy, which routine interictal recordings cannot do. Confident diagnosis then permits antiseizure medication withdrawal and referral for the psychological treatment that actually works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Increase levetiracetam to the maximum tolerated dose
options.rationale: Dose escalation is reasonable in drug resistant epilepsy, but two agents at therapeutic doses with no effect at all should prompt review of the diagnosis rather than further escalation. Levetiracetam at higher doses also causes irritability and mood disturbance that complicate the psychiatric picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and discharge from neurology
options.rationale: Treating a presumed psychiatric cause before the diagnosis is established, and discharging her from neurology in the same breath, is the pathway that leaves patients feeling disbelieved and is associated with poor engagement and poor outcomes. Roughly 10 to 20 per cent of people with functional seizures also have epilepsy, so neurological involvement must continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat the routine electroencephalogram with sleep deprivation
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation raises the yield of interictal epileptiform discharges, but a normal interictal recording never excludes epilepsy and an abnormal one never proves that a given event was epileptic. Only capturing an actual event with simultaneous recording answers the question being asked. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Functional seizures, also called psychogenic non-epileptic seizures or dissociative seizures, account for a substantial proportion of referrals to epilepsy clinics and average several years from onset to diagnosis, during which patients accumulate antiseizure medications, emergency presentations and intubations. Semiological features that favour a functional cause include prolonged duration beyond 2 minutes, forced eye closure with resistance to opening, side to side head or body movement, out of phase limb movements, waxing and waning intensity, preserved awareness during a bilateral motor event and immediate reorientation afterwards. No single feature is diagnostic, which is why video electroencephalographic capture of a typical event is the standard. The diagnosis should be delivered as a positive one with an explanation of mechanism, since how it is communicated strongly predicts engagement, and treatment is psychological, with cognitive behavioural therapy having the best evidence.
key_points: Video electroencephalographic capture of a typical event is the diagnostic standard
Forced eye closure, out of phase movements, long duration and retained awareness favour functional seizures
A normal interictal electroencephalogram neither confirms nor excludes epilepsy
Around 10 to 20 per cent of patients have both functional seizures and epilepsy
Delivery of the diagnosis as a positive explanation predicts engagement and outcome
explanation.pearls: Serum prolactin roughly doubles within 10 to 20 minutes of a generalised tonic clonic seizure and returns to baseline by an hour, so a normal level in a sample taken in that window argues against a generalised convulsion but cannot exclude a focal seizure.

subtopic_detail: Emergent depressive symptoms with passive suicidal ideation during isotretinoin treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old boy brought by his mother, 8 weeks into a course of isotretinoin prescribed by a dermatologist for severe nodulocystic acne. His skin has improved considerably.

His mother says he has withdrawn to his room, resigned from his football team and is sleeping 12 hours a night. When you see him alone he says he feels flat most of the day, has stopped enjoying anything, and over the past fortnight has had recurring thoughts that his family would be better off without him, although he has no plan and has not acted on them. He has never been depressed before and uses no alcohol or drugs.

data_table.Mental state: Reduced eye contact, slowed speech, restricted affect, pervasive anhedonia, passive suicidal ideation with no plan, intent or preparatory acts, no psychotic features
data_table.Examination: Marked improvement in facial and truncal acne, weight stable, no dry mucous membranes requiring treatment change, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests, fasting lipids and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that the evidence shows no causal link and continue
options.rationale: Population level studies have not established that isotretinoin causes depression, and severe acne is itself strongly associated with depression, but that uncertainty does not license continuing the drug in an individual who has developed a depressive episode with suicidal thoughts during treatment. Australian product information directs cessation if significant psychiatric symptoms emerge. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: There is no evidence that psychiatric adverse effects attributed to isotretinoin are dose dependent in a way that dose reduction would mitigate. Four weeks is also too long an interval for a young person with new passive suicidal ideation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily and continue the isotretinoin course
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first line antidepressant for adolescent depression, but starting it while continuing a drug that may be contributing removes the opportunity to see whether symptoms resolve on cessation. Antidepressants in adolescents also carry a small increase in suicidal ideation in the early weeks and require close monitoring rather than being added without specialist assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the course and arrange dermatology review within a month
options.rationale: Deferring the decision to the prescribing specialist is appropriate for questions about the acne, but the treating doctor in front of a young person with new suicidal ideation is responsible for acting on that today. A month of continued treatment leaves both the exposure and the risk unaddressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease isotretinoin now and arrange urgent mental health assessment
options.rationale: Emergence of a depressive episode with suicidal ideation during isotretinoin treatment is an indication to stop the drug promptly and to assess the mental state properly, regardless of what the epidemiological literature says about causation at a population level. Stopping also provides diagnostic information, since symptoms that resolve after withdrawal point to a drug effect while symptoms that persist confirm an independent depressive episode needing treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Isotretinoin carries a longstanding association with depression, psychosis and suicide in case reports and regulatory reporting, while large cohort studies have not demonstrated a causal population level effect and several show improved mood as severe acne clears. Both things can be true, and the practical consequence is that prescribers screen for psychiatric history before starting, counsel the patient and family about what to watch for, and stop the drug if significant symptoms emerge. Severe acne independently carries substantial psychological morbidity, so the presence of depression is never automatic evidence of a drug effect, and a young person whose symptoms persist after cessation needs treatment in his own right. Withdrawal also gives useful information, since resolution within weeks supports a drug contribution. Every adolescent presenting with new depressive symptoms needs to be seen alone for part of the consultation, since suicidal ideation is frequently disclosed only then.
key_points: Causation at a population level is unproven, but individual cessation is indicated when significant symptoms emerge
Severe acne independently carries high psychological morbidity
See the adolescent alone: suicidal ideation is often disclosed only without a parent present
Symptom resolution after withdrawal supports a drug contribution; persistence means treat the depression
Screen for psychiatric history and counsel about warning signs before the drug is started
explanation.pearls: Isotretinoin is teratogenic and requires two forms of contraception and monthly pregnancy testing in anyone who could become pregnant, continuing for one month after the course ends; the same counselling visit is the place to set out the psychiatric warning signs.

subtopic_detail: Progressive drowsiness and vomiting on valproate with a therapeutic level and normal liver function
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the ward to see a 34 year old man admitted 3 weeks ago with a manic episode. His sodium valproate was increased from 500 mg to 1000 mg twice daily 9 days ago and his mania has settled.

Over the past 5 days the nursing staff have noticed he is increasingly drowsy, has vomited three times, and today could not tell them the day or the month. He has had no fever, no headache, no neck stiffness and no seizure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, disoriented to time, asterixis present on outstretched hands, no focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 620 micromol/L (therapeutic range 350 to 700), ALT 28 units/L (less than 40), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), INR 1.0, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), venous ammonia 98 micromol/L (less than 50), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attribute the drowsiness to sedation and reduce the evening dose
options.rationale: Simple sedation does not cause vomiting, disorientation or asterixis, and asterixis in particular is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy rather than drug sedation. Reducing the dose leaves an encephalopathic patient on the drug causing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the head and a lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Imaging and cerebrospinal fluid examination are appropriate when there is fever, meningism, focal signs, head injury or no metabolic explanation, and here a clear metabolic cause has already been demonstrated. Proceeding to lumbar puncture first delays withdrawal of the causative drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cease sodium valproate and monitor ammonia and conscious state
options.rationale: Valproate induced hyperammonaemic encephalopathy occurs through inhibition of the urea cycle and is independent of both hepatic injury and serum drug concentration, which is why the normal liver function tests and therapeutic level do not exclude it. It reverses over days once the drug is withdrawn, and ammonia and conscious state are followed to confirm recovery. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue valproate since the serum level is within the target range
options.rationale: The syndrome is not concentration dependent and occurs at levels well within the therapeutic range, so a reassuring level is the single most common reason the diagnosis is missed. Continuing exposure risks progression to coma and cerebral oedema. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give lorazepam 1 mg for agitation and review in the morning
options.rationale: He is drowsy rather than agitated, and adding a sedative to a patient with a declining conscious level risks respiratory compromise and obscures the trend being monitored. It also treats a symptom he does not have. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate induced hyperammonaemic encephalopathy presents subacutely with drowsiness, vomiting, confusion, ataxia and asterixis, and it is regularly missed because both the liver function tests and the serum valproate concentration are normal. The mechanism is inhibition of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase within the urea cycle and depletion of carnitine, not hepatocellular injury, which is a separate and rarer valproate toxicity with deranged transaminases and coagulopathy. Risk is increased by concurrent topiramate or carbamazepine, by carnitine deficiency and by an underlying urea cycle disorder, which should be considered when the syndrome occurs at low doses or recurs. Treatment is withdrawal of valproate with supportive care, and L-carnitine is used in severe or slowly resolving cases. Recovery over several days is the rule, and the episode should be documented prominently because rechallenge reproduces it.
key_points: Normal liver function tests and a therapeutic valproate level do not exclude the diagnosis
Asterixis with drowsiness and vomiting should prompt an ammonia measurement
The mechanism is urea cycle inhibition, not hepatotoxicity
Topiramate and carbamazepine co-prescription increase the risk
Withdrawal of valproate reverses the syndrome over days; L-carnitine is used if severe
explanation.pearls: Measure venous ammonia in any patient on valproate who becomes confused or drowsy, taking the sample without a tourniquet and transporting it on ice, because a delayed or haemolysed specimen gives a falsely elevated result that sends the workup in the wrong direction.

subtopic_detail: Additive upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk from a serotonergic antidepressant with dual antiplatelet therapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 68 year old man who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years for recurrent depression, currently in remission. Eight months ago he had a drug eluting stent inserted and takes aspirin 100 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg daily.

He mentions three weeks of burning discomfort behind the lower sternum, worse after meals. He has had no vomiting, no difficulty swallowing, no weight loss and has not noticed any black or bloody stool. He takes no anti-inflammatory medicines.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness with no guarding, no mass, rectal examination shows brown stool negative on faecal occult blood testing
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130 to 180), mean cell volume 89 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30 to 300), urea and electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: Which single change is most likely to reduce his risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding?

options.text: Stop aspirin and continue clopidogrel as single antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: Shortening dual antiplatelet therapy is a cardiology decision that balances stent thrombosis against bleeding, and stopping an agent 8 months after a drug eluting stent without that assessment risks a catastrophic thrombotic event. It also removes protection he needs rather than adding protection he lacks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor alongside his current medicines
options.rationale: He carries three additive risk factors for upper gastrointestinal bleeding, namely dual antiplatelet therapy, age over 65 and a serotonergic antidepressant, which impairs platelet serotonin uptake and therefore platelet aggregation. Co-prescribing acid suppression is the intervention with the clearest evidence of benefit in this combination and does not require removing any of the drugs he needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Switch sertraline to another selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: The bleeding risk arises from serotonin reuptake inhibition itself, so switching within the same class carries the risk across rather than removing it. If an antidepressant change were pursued, the logic would point to an agent with minimal serotonergic activity, and his depression is currently in remission on this one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose and review his mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is not established to reduce bleeding risk meaningfully and jeopardises remission in recurrent depression, where relapse after dose reduction is common. It trades a proven psychiatric benefit for an unproven gastrointestinal one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Replace aspirin and clopidogrel with a direct oral anticoagulant
options.rationale: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are not interchangeable: direct oral anticoagulants do not prevent stent thrombosis in place of dual antiplatelet therapy, and they carry their own substantial gastrointestinal bleeding risk. This is the near pair worth keeping straight, since both drug classes reduce thrombosis but through different pathways and for different indications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Platelets do not synthesise serotonin but take it up from plasma using the same transporter that serotonergic antidepressants block, so these drugs deplete platelet serotonin and impair aggregation, producing a measurable increase in bleeding risk. Alone the absolute risk is small, but it multiplies when combined with antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, older age or previous ulcer disease. The practical response is not usually to stop the antidepressant, but to recognise the stacking of risks and to add gastroprotection, which is well evidenced in patients on dual antiplatelet therapy. Dyspepsia in this context also warrants consideration of Helicobacter pylori testing, and any alarm feature such as anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, vomiting or melaena would change the plan to endoscopy. The same interaction should be considered before surgery, where perioperative bleeding risk is modestly increased.
key_points: Serotonergic antidepressants impair platelet aggregation by depleting platelet serotonin
Risk multiplies with antiplatelets, anticoagulants, anti-inflammatories, age and prior ulcer
Proton pump inhibitor co-prescription is the best evidenced mitigation on dual antiplatelet therapy
Switching within the serotonergic class carries the risk across rather than removing it
Alarm features mandate endoscopy rather than empirical acid suppression
explanation.pearls: When a proton pump inhibitor is needed alongside clopidogrel, choose pantoprazole or rabeprazole rather than omeprazole or esomeprazole, because the latter two inhibit cytochrome P450 2C19 and reduce conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite.

subtopic_detail: Escalating gaming and school refusal in an adolescent as avoidance driven by an anxiety disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15 year old boy whose parents are worried that he games for around 10 hours a day and has not attended school for 6 weeks. He becomes irritable when they take the console away and has stopped seeing the friends he used to skate with, although he speaks nightly to the same group online.

Seen alone, he tells you he stopped going after a class presentation where he lost his place and some students laughed. He now feels sick and shaky from the moment he wakes on a school day, dreads being looked at in the corridor, and lies awake going over things he has said. He says gaming is the only time his mind is quiet.

data_table.Mental state: Anxious affect, no pervasive low mood, no anhedonia outside school related activities, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, insight into the pattern of avoidance
data_table.History: No alcohol or drug use, no gambling or in-game purchasing, no bullying reported beyond the presentation incident, was a competent student until this term
data_table.Examination: Physical examination normal, growth tracking on the 50th centile, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Set a graded screen time limit contract and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Removing the avoidance behaviour without addressing the anxiety driving it typically increases distress and conflict, because gaming is functioning as the only regulation strategy he has. Screen limits belong in a treatment plan, not as the intervention in place of one. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Diagnose internet gaming disorder and refer for addiction counselling
options.rationale: Internet gaming disorder remains a condition for further study rather than an established diagnosis, and it should not be applied when the gaming is better explained by another disorder. Here the gaming began after a specific social humiliation and functions as avoidance and relief, which points to the anxiety as primary. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Commence melatonin 2 mg at night to correct the sleep cycle first
options.rationale: His difficulty getting to sleep reflects rumination and anxiety rather than a primary circadian disorder, and treating the sleep symptom leaves the driver untouched. Melatonin has a role in delayed sleep phase and in some neurodevelopmental conditions, neither of which is described. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Assess for an anxiety disorder driving the school avoidance
options.rationale: The history contains the defining features of social anxiety disorder, namely marked fear of scrutiny with anticipatory physical symptoms, post-event rumination and avoidance that began after a specific humiliating experience. Assessing and treating the anxiety, typically with cognitive behavioural therapy and a graded return to school, addresses the cause of both the absence and the gaming. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Refer the family for therapy focused on parental limit setting
options.rationale: Family work is often a valuable component, particularly where accommodation of avoidance has become entrenched, but making limit setting the focus frames the problem as a discipline issue. That framing tends to escalate conflict and delays recognition of the treatable anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

explanation.summary: Excessive gaming in adolescence is far more often a symptom than a disorder, and the clinical task is to work out what it is doing for the young person. School refusal in particular is usually anxiety driven and is distinguished from truancy by the fact that the young person stays home with the parents' knowledge, is distressed rather than delinquent, and often has physical symptoms on school mornings that resolve at weekends. Social anxiety disorder frequently begins in early adolescence, is often precipitated by a humiliating event, and is characterised by fear of scrutiny, anticipatory symptoms and post-event rumination. Treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with graded exposure and a structured return to school negotiated with the school, with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor added where symptoms are severe or therapy alone is insufficient. Duration of absence is the strongest predictor of outcome, so early intervention matters.
key_points: School refusal is distinguished from truancy by parental knowledge, distress and morning somatic symptoms
Excessive gaming is more often avoidance or self-regulation than a primary disorder
Social anxiety disorder features fear of scrutiny, anticipatory symptoms and post-event rumination
Cognitive behavioural therapy with graded school return is first line
Longer absence predicts worse outcome, so early intervention matters
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the somatic symptoms occur at weekends and in school holidays: symptoms that disappear on non-school days point firmly to anxiety driven school refusal rather than to a physical illness needing further investigation.

subtopic_detail: Massive modified release paracetamol ingestion where a level below the nomogram line does not exclude toxicity
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 19 year old woman brought in by her housemate 5 hours after she swallowed a bottle of tablets following the end of a relationship. She now regrets it and is cooperative.

The pack is a modified release paracetamol preparation containing 665 mg per tablet, and 40 tablets are missing. She weighs 55 kg, has vomited once, and has taken no other substance and no alcohol. Her housemate confirms the timing. A blood sample drawn at 4 hours after ingestion has returned, and the resident has plotted it below the treatment line and suggests she be referred to the mental health team for discharge planning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and fully oriented, no abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, no asterixis, no evidence of other ingestion
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol concentration at 4 hours after ingestion 110 mg/L, ALT 22 units/L (less than 40), INR 1.0, creatinine 64 micromol/L (45 to 90), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22 to 32), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge her as the four hour level sits below the treatment line
options.rationale: The treatment nomogram is validated for a single acute ingestion of an immediate release preparation, and it cannot be applied to a modified release formulation, in which continued absorption produces a later peak and a concentration that can cross the line hours after a reassuring early sample. Discharging on that basis is the specific error this presentation is built around. (Source: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline)

options.text: Give activated charcoal now and repeat the paracetamol level at 12 hours
options.rationale: Activated charcoal retains a role in massive or modified release ingestion and may be given beyond the usual 2 hour window, so it is a reasonable adjunct rather than a wrong action, but it is not the priority and cannot substitute for the antidote. Waiting until 12 hours for the next concentration also abandons the paired sampling interval that guides treatment. (Source: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline)

options.text: Commence acetylcysteine now and repeat the level in 4 hours
options.rationale: Forty tablets of 665 mg is 26.6 g, which at 55 kg is about 480 mg/kg and therefore a massive ingestion well beyond the threshold at which acetylcysteine is started regardless of the concentration. For modified release preparations two levels are taken 4 hours apart and treatment continues if either crosses the line, because absorption is ongoing and the first sample can be falsely reassuring. (Source: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline)

options.text: Withhold treatment and recheck the level and liver tests at 8 hours
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine is close to fully protective when started within 8 hours of ingestion and its efficacy declines steadily thereafter, so deferring it to await a second result spends the window in which it works best. Normal liver enzymes at 5 hours are expected and carry no reassurance, since transaminase elevation typically appears after 24 hours. (Source: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline)

options.text: Measure the international normalised ratio and treat only if it rises
options.rationale: Coagulopathy is a marker of established hepatic injury rather than a trigger for prophylaxis, and by the time the international normalised ratio rises the toxic metabolite has already bound hepatocyte proteins. Treating on that basis converts a preventable poisoning into an established liver injury. (Source: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline)

explanation.summary: Paracetamol is the most common agent in deliberate self-poisoning in Australia and is usually managed algorithmically, which is precisely why the exceptions to the algorithm cause harm. The standard treatment nomogram applies only to a single acute ingestion of an immediate release preparation at a known time, and it is invalid for modified release formulations, staggered ingestions and ingestions of unknown timing. Modified release paracetamol continues to be absorbed for many hours, so a concentration drawn at 4 hours may sit below the line while the true peak arrives later, and Australian guidance therefore requires two levels 4 hours apart with treatment continued if either exceeds the line. A separate dose based trigger applies irrespective of concentration for massive ingestion, and very large ingestions may also require an increased acetylcysteine infusion rate. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is close to completely hepatoprotective when begun within 8 hours, which makes early commencement more valuable than diagnostic certainty, and the psychiatric assessment that must follow is additional to medical stabilisation rather than a substitute for it.
key_points: The nomogram is invalid for modified release, staggered and unknown time ingestions
Modified release ingestions require two levels 4 hours apart, treating if either crosses the line
Massive ingestion triggers acetylcysteine on dose alone, regardless of concentration
Acetylcysteine is close to fully protective within 8 hours and declines thereafter
Normal transaminases early after ingestion carry no reassurance, as injury appears after 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Always ask which paracetamol preparation was taken and check the pack, because modified release tablets are commonly sold as 665 mg osteoarthritis formulations and are the single most important reason a paracetamol overdose is under-treated on a reassuring early level.

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness with a heliotrope and knuckle rash persisting after statin withdrawal
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 56 year old woman with 4 months of increasing difficulty rising from a low chair and hanging washing on the line. She has to push up on the arms of her chair and can no longer reach the top shelf of her cupboard.

Her general practitioner stopped her atorvastatin 8 weeks ago for presumed statin related muscle pain, with no improvement since. Over the past 6 weeks she has developed a purple discolouration of both upper eyelids and scaly red plaques over the knuckles of both hands. She has no dysphagia and no breathlessness.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness with power 3 out of 5 at both hip flexors and 4 out of 5 at both shoulder abductors, distal power preserved, reflexes and sensation normal, violaceous discolouration of both upper eyelids, scaly erythematous plaques over the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 2840 units/L (30 to 200), ALT 92 units/L (less than 40), ESR 44 mm/h (less than 20), TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45 to 90), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to rheumatology and arrange malignancy screening
options.rationale: Symmetrical proximal weakness with a markedly raised creatine kinase, a violaceous eyelid rash and scaly plaques over the knuckles is an inflammatory myopathy with a characteristic cutaneous pattern, and in adults this carries a substantially increased risk of an underlying cancer, concentrated in the three years either side of diagnosis. Age and sex appropriate screening, including breast, gynaecological, bowel and lung assessment, therefore runs alongside specialist referral rather than after it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies)

options.text: Recheck the creatine kinase in 8 weeks now the statin has stopped
options.rationale: Statin related myalgia usually settles within 4 to 6 weeks of withdrawal, and hers has not improved after 8 weeks while a rash has appeared, so the statin has already been excluded as the explanation. A further 8 weeks of observation delays treatment of a myopathy that is causing progressive functional loss. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence colchicine and refer to dermatology for the skin rash
options.rationale: Colchicine treats crystal arthropathy, which produces acutely painful inflamed joints rather than painless symmetrical proximal weakness, and there is no synovitis. Referring the rash separately also splits a single systemic diagnosis into two unrelated problems. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the legs
options.rationale: Electromyography does support the diagnosis by showing a myopathic pattern with spontaneous activity, and it is part of the specialist workup alongside myositis specific antibodies, magnetic resonance imaging and sometimes muscle biopsy. Ordering it as the next step from a general clinic delays both the referral and the cancer screening that most changes her outcome. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Inflammatory myopathies)

options.text: Restart a lower dose statin and monitor the creatine kinase level
options.rationale: Rechallenge at a lower dose is a reasonable strategy for genuine statin intolerance once the creatine kinase has normalised off the drug. Here the enzyme remains more than ten times the upper limit of normal off treatment, which points away from a simple statin effect and makes rechallenge unsafe. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: The idiopathic inflammatory myopathies present with painless symmetrical proximal weakness developing over weeks to months, and patients describe function rather than weakness, reporting difficulty with stairs, rising from chairs, washing hair or reaching overhead. A raised creatine kinase supports muscle inflammation, but the level correlates poorly with severity and normal values do not exclude the diagnosis, particularly in the amyopathic variant where skin disease dominates. The cutaneous signs are the most useful discriminator at the bedside, with a violaceous periorbital rash and scaly plaques over the extensor surfaces of the finger joints being characteristic, and they separate this from polymyositis, statin associated myopathy, hypothyroid myopathy and inclusion body myositis. Adults with the dermatomyositis pattern carry a several fold increased risk of malignancy, highest in the year before and the two years after diagnosis, so screening is a routine part of initial management rather than a response to suspicious features. Assessment also covers swallowing and respiratory muscle involvement and interstitial lung disease, both of which drive early mortality.
key_points: Patients report functional difficulty rather than weakness, so ask about stairs, chairs and hair washing
Creatine kinase level correlates poorly with severity and can be normal in amyopathic disease
A violaceous eyelid rash with scaly plaques over the finger joints is the key bedside discriminator
Adult dermatomyositis carries a several fold increased malignancy risk requiring routine screening
Assess swallowing, respiratory muscle strength and interstitial lung disease at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Weakness that is asymmetrical, involves finger flexors and quadriceps, and progresses over years in a man over 50 points to inclusion body myositis, which barely responds to corticosteroid and is the commonest reason an inflammatory myopathy appears treatment resistant.

subtopic_detail: Dysphagia to solids and liquids with nocturnal regurgitation and a normal gastroscopy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 44 year old woman with 18 months of food sticking in her lower chest. She initially managed by drinking water with meals, but over the past few months liquids have become just as difficult as solids.

She wakes at night coughing and finds undigested food from the previous evening on her pillow. She has lost 5 kg. She was treated with a proton pump inhibitor for a year without benefit.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no abdominal mass
data_table.Gastroscopy: Dilated oesophageal body containing retained food and saliva, normal mucosa with no stricture, ulcer or mass, gastro-oesophageal junction traversed with mild resistance, biopsies of the distal oesophagus showed no eosinophilic infiltrate
data_table.Barium swallow: Smooth tapering of the distal oesophagus with proximal dilatation and delayed emptying of contrast

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Commence high dose proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks and review
options.rationale: Acid suppression is a reasonable empirical trial for reflux related symptoms, and she has already had a full year without benefit. Dysphagia that progresses to affect liquids equally is an alarm symptom that requires a diagnosis rather than another therapeutic trial. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Refer for laparoscopic fundoplication to control the regurgitation
options.rationale: Fundoplication increases resistance at the gastro-oesophageal junction, which is precisely the problem in a patient who cannot relax that sphincter, and would worsen the obstruction. This is an important near pair: the regurgitation of undigested food from a dilated oesophagus is not the acid reflux that fundoplication treats. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest with oral contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is used to exclude a malignancy infiltrating the gastro-oesophageal junction, which produces a similar picture known as pseudoachalasia, and is considered when the history is short, weight loss is marked or the patient is older. Endoscopy has already shown normal mucosa with no mass, and imaging alone cannot assess sphincter function. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with biopsies of the distal oesophagus
options.rationale: Repeat endoscopic sampling would be indicated if eosinophilic oesophagitis were still suspected, but that produces dysphagia to solids with food bolus impaction rather than equal difficulty with liquids, and the biopsies were already negative. Endoscopy is normal in a substantial proportion of patients with this motility disorder, so repeating it adds nothing. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry studies
options.rationale: Dysphagia that affects liquids as much as solids indicates a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction, and manometry is the diagnostic standard, demonstrating absent peristalsis with failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax. It also assigns the manometric subtype, which determines whether pneumatic dilatation, myotomy or peroral endoscopic myotomy is likely to succeed. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

explanation.summary: The first branch point in dysphagia is whether the difficulty is with solids alone, which suggests a mechanical narrowing, or with solids and liquids equally, which points to a motility disorder. Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with absent peristalsis, and it typically presents over months to years with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain and weight loss. Patients are frequently treated for reflux for years before the diagnosis is made, and the failure of acid suppression is itself a clue. Endoscopy is mandatory to exclude malignancy at the gastro-oesophageal junction, which can mimic achalasia exactly, but it is often normal, and high resolution manometry establishes the diagnosis and the subtype. Treatment options are pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy, and botulinum toxin injection for those unfit for definitive treatment.
key_points: Dysphagia to liquids as well as solids indicates a motility disorder, not a stricture
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Endoscopy is required to exclude malignancy mimicking achalasia but is often normal
Years of failed acid suppression before diagnosis is the typical history
Fundoplication worsens the obstruction and is not a treatment for this condition
explanation.pearls: Suspect pseudoachalasia from tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction when symptoms have lasted under a year, weight loss is disproportionate or the patient is over 55, and obtain cross sectional imaging before committing to dilatation or myotomy.
